title: Inodes, Hard Links vs Symbolic Links & Zero-Downtime Atomic Deployments
why_it_matters: Have you ever seen `No space left on device` on a server when `df -h` says 40% of the disk is still free? Or wondered how tools like Capistrano and Nginx switch releases with zero downtime? Both come down to understanding Inodes, Hard Links, and Symbolic Links (`ln -sfn`).
concept_explanation: 1. What Is an Inode? On a Linux filesystem (`ext4`, `xfs`), a file's *name* is NOT stored inside the file. Instead, a directory is just a lookup table mapping `filename -> inode number`. The **inode** stores all metadata: file size, owner UID/GID, permissions, timestamps, link count, and pointers to the actual data blocks on disk.

2. Inode Exhaustion (`df -i`): Every filesystem has a fixed or limited pool of inodes. If a poorly written app or cache creates millions of tiny 1-byte files, you will run out of inodes (`IUse% = 100%` in `df -i`) and Linux will throw `No space left on device` even with gigabytes of free block storage!

3. Hard Links (`ln target link_name`):
   - Creates a second directory entry pointing to the **exact same inode number**.
   - Deleting the original file (`rm target`) does NOT delete the data blocks as long as the inode's link count > 0 (and no process has the file open).
   - Limitations: Cannot cross filesystem/partition boundaries, and cannot link directories.

4. Symbolic / Soft Links (`ln -s target link_name`):
   - Creates a brand new file with its **own inode** whose content is simply the text path to the target.
   - Can point to directories and across different disks/mounts.
   - If the target is deleted, the symlink becomes 'dangling' (broken).

5. DevOps Pattern — Atomic Symlink Switching: To deploy `release-v2` without downtime while processes read `/var/www/current`, you deploy to `/var/www/releases/v2` and run `ln -sfn /var/www/releases/v2 /var/www/current`.
cheat_sheet: ls -li                      # Show inode numbers (-i) alongside permissions and link counts
stat config.yaml            # Full inode metadata: size, blocks, inode #, links, mtime/ctime/atime
df -i                       # Check inode usage percentage across all mounted filesystems
ln source.txt hardlink.txt  # Create a hard link (same inode)

lab.title: Perform an Atomic Symlink Release Cutover & Hard-Link Backup
lab.description: Practice working with inodes, hard links, and atomic symlink release switching inside `workspace/devops/day-003`:
tasks: 1. Run `./grow lab 3` to set up `workspace/devops/day-003` containing `releases/v1.0.0/version.txt`, `releases/v2.0.0/version.txt`, and `shared/database.sqlite`.
2. Right now, `current` is a symlink pointing to `releases/v1.0.0`. Update the `current` symlink so it points to `releases/v2.0.0` (so `cat current/version.txt` outputs `v2.0.0`).
3. Create a **hard link** named `shared/database.sqlite.bak` pointing to the exact same inode as `shared/database.sqlite`.
4. Find the inode number of `shared/database.sqlite` (using `stat -c %i` or `ls -i`) and write ONLY that integer number into `workspace/devops/day-003/db_inode.txt`.

verifications.description: 'current' is a symbolic link resolving to releases/v2.0.0
shared/database.sqlite.bak is a hard link sharing the exact same inode as shared/database.sqlite
db_inode.txt contains the exact inode number of shared/database.sqlite

quiz.question: A production server alerts with `No space left on device` when creating a file, but `df -h` shows 65 GB free on `/`. Which command should you run next to check if millions of tiny files exhausted the filesystem metadata table?
options: A) free -h
B) df -i
C) du -sh /
D) lsblk
quiz.explanation: `df -i` displays inode usage. If `IUse%` is 100%, no new files can be created regardless of how many gigabytes of block space remain.

quiz.question: Which piece of information is NOT stored inside a file's inode?
options: A) Owner UID and GID
B) File permissions (mode)
C) The file's name
D) Pointers to the data blocks on disk
quiz.explanation: Filenames are stored in directory entries (which map filename -> inode number), NOT in the inode itself. That's why a single inode can have multiple filenames (hard links) pointing to it.

quiz.question: You create a hard link `ln app.log app_backup.log` and then delete `rm app.log`. What happens to `app_backup.log` and the underlying data?
options: A) `app_backup.log` becomes a broken link and the data is lost
B) The inode's link count decrements from 2 to 1, and `app_backup.log` retains full access to the intact data
C) Both files are deleted automatically
D) `app_backup.log` is truncated to 0 bytes
quiz.explanation: Data blocks are only freed when an inode's link count drops to 0 AND no running process has an open file descriptor to that inode.

quiz.question: Why can't you create a hard link from `/home/user/file.txt` to `/mnt/external_disk/file.txt`?
options: A) Hard links require root privileges
B) Inode numbers are only unique within a single mounted filesystem; hard links cannot cross filesystem boundaries
C) `/mnt` is read-only by default
D) Hard links only work on `.sh` files
quiz.explanation: Each mounted filesystem maintains its own independent inode table (so inode #500 on `/` is completely unrelated to inode #500 on `/mnt/external_disk`). Only symbolic links (`ln -s`) can cross filesystems.

quiz.question: A running Java service has a 20 GB log file `/var/log/app.log` open. A developer runs `rm /var/log/app.log` to free disk space, but `df -h` shows the 20 GB was NOT freed! Why?
options: A) `rm` moves files to `/root/.Trash` first
B) Although the directory link count reached 0, the running Java process still holds an open file descriptor to that inode until the process restarts or the file is truncated (`truncate -s 0`)
C) ext4 only frees space after a reboot
D) You must run `sync` three times
quiz.explanation: This is one of the most common DevOps interview and production questions! The kernel only reclaims blocks when BOTH the link count is 0 AND open file descriptor count is 0. You can see deleted-but-open files with `lsof +L1`.
